#StreetAccount Summary - Asia Annual Recap (2025)

Overview:

Equities:

• Asia equities ended a stellar if at times volatile year near record highs as AI-related technologies and dovish central bank trends more than offset concerns over tech stock valuations and US tariffs. The MSCI Asia Pac ex Japan index added 26.8% while Japan's Nikkei and Topix boards rose for a third consecutive year as its stockmarket 'value-up' program accelerated and corporate earnings proved robust against tariffs, BOJ rate hikes and a weaker yen.
• However, the strong year also included the largest equity market selloff since the pandemic after President Trump in April launched a set of tariffs that threated to trigger a global recession. The original structure was quickly watered down and followed by a series of state- and sector-wide deals while the feared recession never materialized. Indeed, economic growth proved better than expected almost everywhere except Japan and China, where buoyant exports were offset by slower output and retail sales growth, another decline in house prices and a collapse in investment.
• Despite the economic wobbles, mainland China's stock markets rallied to their best year in eight thanks to government backing via 'national team' buying, a steadily strengthening yuan, and optimism over technology innovation. Enthusiasm for DeepSeek's AI model sparked the positive run but not before record low bond yields and deflationary pressures helped push equities lower early on. The tech-led rally stalled out somewhat in Q4 over broad economic concerns but analysts still forecast a positive 2026 for China-based equities. The Hang Seng posted a 27% y/y advance, boosted by easing trade tensions and a buoyant IPO market.
• South Korea's Kospi was the best performing major country benchmark globally with a 79.5% gain. SK Hynix (000660.KS) surged 283% and Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) 130% on AI chip demand and accounted for almost half of the Kospi's gains but there were also significant advances in defense, shipbuilding and nuclear power stocks reflecting the shift in global geopolitics and power demand. Taiwan's Taiex ended at record highs as printed circuit board and memory stocks advanced the most in an AI-related rally. The market-cap heavy TSMC (https://t.co/qAnDxBEknJ) returned 44% but it was PCB glass fiber group Glotech Industrial's (https://t.co/1QCv68jkwI) 686% advance and memory giant Nanya Tech's (https://t.co/RjcKSS9pLv) 560% gain that headlined the winners' list.
• Australia's ASX gained 15% as gold and other mining stocks surged on commodity prices but gains were capped by a sharp underperformance in IT names. The markets also had to contend with three RBA rate cuts but a strong signal in December that its next move may be a hike. New Zealand's NZX 50 also gained but underperformed amid persistent worries over economic growth and export exposure to a slowing China.
• India's markets logged a tenth consecutive annual gain amid solid economic fundamentals but underperformed as overseas investors sold a record $18.5B shares to reduce their holdings to a 15-year low and trading activity fell around 20%. The underperformance came after the US imposed a 50% tariff following the failure of trade talks and New Delhi responded with a large-scale GST cut. Concerns over valuations also weighed, especially as corporate earnings started to underwhelm, and yet the market also saw a record $22B raised in IPOs, underscoring domestic investor optimism.
• Singapore's FTSE STI ended at a record high amid stronger-than-expected economic growth and trade concerns that failed to materialize in any meaningful manner. Indonesia's JSX composite posted its best year since 2014 driven by government fiscal spending plans, a dovish Bank Indonesia and advances in conglomerate stocks. Malaysia's KLCI also outperformed amid strong economic growth as the country quickly established itself as ASEAN's data center hub. Thailand's SET fell amid an overseas investor exodus triggered by a strong baht, unstable domestic politics and a border clash with Cambodia. The Philippines PSE also declined amid an expanding graft scandal that also chased away overseas investors.

Bonds

• Bond markets were volatile. Longer-dated bond yields fell sharply after Trump unveiled his tariffs regime in April which fed into the inflation narrative and the potential for delays to rate cuts. These quickly reversed once a pause was announced and trade deals signed, sparking a sharp upturn in Asia yields. The rise in long-dated JGB yields were especially acute as the BOJ hiked rates twice and new PM Takaichi unveiled a ¥21.3T ($137B) stimulus package that included a ¥6.9T provision for new bond issuance.
• Elsewhere, there are strong indications Asia central banks will end their easing cycles in 2026 due to stubborn inflation or, in the case of the BOK, sky-high house prices. The RBA's hawkish pivot pushed Australian sovereigns yields to two-year highs and South Korea 10Y yields to 18-month highs. Even CGB 10Y yields rose y/y amid a strong equity market rally, easing trade tensions with the US and recovering economic sentiment although gains were capped after Beijing gave strong indications it would rely on fiscal policy over monetary easing next year to support its economy. IGBs sank as US trade negotiations broke down and the government cut GST, recovering after strong economic data appeared to defy Trump's tariffs and the RBI resumed its rate cut cycle.

Currencies:

• Asia currencies rallied in aggregate but were volatile amid a 9.5% decline in the US dollar, its sharpest y/y fall in eight years. The yen traded almost flat y/y, strengthening to around 140 per dollar into the 'Liberation Day' tariffs before falling back to the start line at around 156. Although two BOJ rate hikes should have sparked a yen appreciation, they were offset by the likelihood of further hikes being drawn out, the government's spending plans, and the potential for the next move in other central banks ex the US to be a hike.
• The yuan had one of its best years in decades as trade relations with the US improved and economic sentiment improved, ending just below 7.0 per dollar. The Taiwan dollar outperformed amid elevated exports to the US and domestic life insurers that hedged against a weak US dollar, although the latter did so at such a pace the central bank was forced to intervene several times. The won depreciated to levels last seen in the GFC on investor outflow and worries over the $350B investment component of its US trade deal. But it rallied in December after authorities warned of direct intervention and introduced several soft controls.
• The Australian dollar was a standout, rallying almost 8% y/y as the RBA pivoted away from easing amid robust economic figures. The New Zealand dollar also rallied as economists speculated the RBNZ was nearing the end of its easing cycle and its economy showed signs of improvement.
• The rupee was the region's worst performer as the US's 50% tariff rate started to bite. This encouraged overseas investors to exit domestic markets while the prospect of losing remittance payments post US visa changes also weighed. The RBI heavily intervened on several occasions, supporting via the sale of around $30B in foreign currencies. Thailand's baht was the region's best performer as it rode the gold surge but fell late in the year after the central bank issued several warnings. Malaysia's ringgit outperformed with a more than 10% gain on rising FDI especially in data centers, and the government's drive on fiscal consolidation. Underperformers included the Indonesian rupiah which fell on worries over the new government's fiscal spending bill, and the Philippine peso that declined on a growing investor exodus post a large-scale graft scandal.

Catalysts:

• President Trump launched his 'Liberation Day' tariff program in early April with the size and scope of the levies surprising almost everyone. It sparked a sudden equity market selloff but once Treasuries began to wobble, the White House paused to allow for deal negotiations to begin, leading to an equally strong equity rally. Asia nations one-by-one signed watered-down deals with most settling on a 19-20% rate although South Korea and Japan negotiated 15% plus substantial investment commitments, and Singapore and Australia 10%. China's tariff stood briefly at 145% before Presidents Trump and Xi negotiated a truce, a 10% base rate and a fentanyl surcharge that were offset by several sectoral deals including one on advanced chip supplies from Nvidia. An exception remains India, which still sits with a 50% rate amid an absence of a deal.
• Asia economic performance surprised to the upside with many central banks raising FY forecasts several times. Two exceptions were Japan, which looks set to see below average growth rate for the full year, and China. Here, nominal GDP growth slowed for each of the three published quarters while monthly activity data, especially in Q4, showed slower growth. A collapse in investment and declining money supply also point to a contraction in economic activity while consumer deflation is still a threat and the housing market remains dire. Offsetting this, exports remained far more robust than expected. Elsewhere, bleak forecasts of a tariff-induced recession proved unfounded with better-than-expected growth almost everywhere following a Q1 wobble when tariff uncertainty dominated. Technology exports in northern countries pillared economic performance there, while domestic industrial output and consumption supported ASEAN and Australia.
• Asia-ex central banks cut base interest rates in two distinct phases. First, as US trade tariffs were rumored, announced, then imposed; and the second when domestic inflation fell sufficiently for banks to counter wobbles in economic data. But by the year-end there were signals from many, including the BOK and RBA, that their easing cycle was at - or close to - an end and a hike was even possible in 2026. A second theme that emerged was surprises, especially in emerging Asia where several banks, several times surprised with a hold or a cut against expectations because, economists said, of growing economic uncertainties. The PBOC trimmed its base rates just once as Beijing indicated it preferred fiscal stimulus over monetary easing while the outlier was the BOJ, which hiked twice by 25 bps as inflation remained stubbornly high and wage growth continued to inch higher.
• In regional political developments, South Korea elected Democratic Party candidate Lee Jae-myung as President just months after former President Yoon's failed military coup attempt. Japan PM Ishiba resigned after his LDP party suffered a major election defeat in Japan's upper house with Sanae Takaichi eventually elected as its new PM. Thailand's constitutional court stripped PM Paetongtarn Shinawatra of her duties after Cambodia's leader Hun Sen leaked details of a phone call between the two. The call was made in attempt to end a military border clash between the two countries, which simmered for most of H2.

Country Equity Performance (FY 2025):

• Equity markets: MSCI Asia Pacific ex Japan +26.8%; Japan Nikkei +26.6%; Greater China: CSI 300 +22.9%, Shenzhen +35.6%, Hang Seng 27.5%; Australia ASX 200 15.3%; New Zealand NZX50 +6.4%; South Korea Kospi +79.5%; Taiwan Taiex +31.2%; Singapore STI +30.1%; Malaysia KLCI +8.1%; Thailand SET -2.6%; Indonesia JSX +17.9%, Philippines PSI -8.8%; India Sensex +3.4%, Nifty50 +4.8%.
• In USD as of 6.00pm HK/SG time 31 December 2025
